stem: In an ER diagram, a many-to-many relationship between two entities is implemented as

options.text: A separate junction table holding a foreign key to each
A composite primary key on one table
A foreign key on either side

explanation: Neither side can hold a single foreign key without repeating rows, so the relationship becomes its own table. Its primary key is usually the pair of foreign keys, which also enforces uniqueness of the pairing.

stem: A weak entity is one that

options.text: Cannot be identified without its owning entity, so its key includes the owner's
Has no primary key at all

explanation: An order line identified only by line number needs the order id to be unique. The dependency is on identification, not on data volume.

stem: A surrogate key is preferred over a natural key when

options.text: The natural key is large, changeable, or may not exist for every row

explanation: Business identifiers change more often than people expect, and a changing primary key means cascading updates everywhere it is referenced. The cost of a surrogate is an extra column and one more join to read the natural key.

stem: A composite primary key is one that

options.text: Spans two or more columns, which together identify a row uniquely

explanation: Every column in it must still be non-null, and minimality applies: if a subset already identifies the row, the extra column does not belong in the key.

stem: Boyce-Codd normal form is stricter than third normal form in that it requires

options.text: Every determinant to be a candidate key

explanation: 3NF tolerates a non-key determinant when the dependent attribute is part of a candidate key; BCNF does not. The cases that separate them are rare and involve overlapping candidate keys.

stem: Update, insert and delete anomalies all arise from

options.text: Redundancy, where the same fact is stored in more than one place

explanation: Normalisation is the systematic removal of that redundancy, which is why each normal form is defined by the dependency it eliminates rather than by a table count.

stem: Atomicity guarantees that a transaction

options.text: Either completes entirely or has no effect at all

explanation: Partial application is what atomicity forbids, which is why a transfer cannot debit one account without crediting the other. Rollback is the mechanism that delivers it.

stem: Consistency in ACID means a transaction takes the database

options.text: To the same state every time
From one state satisfying all constraints to another such state

explanation: It is about constraints and invariants, not about concurrency or replication. The C in ACID and the C in the CAP theorem name different properties, which is a frequent conflation.

stem: Repeatable Read prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads but may still allow

options.text: Phantom reads, where a re-run query sees newly inserted matching rows

explanation: Row-level stability does not stop new rows appearing in a range. Serializable is the level that excludes phantoms, at a higher concurrency cost.

stem: Optimistic concurrency control works by

options.text: Letting transactions proceed and checking a version at commit, failing if it changed

explanation: It suits low-contention workloads because it avoids holding locks, and pushes the cost onto retrying the rare conflict. Under heavy contention pessimistic locking wins.

stem: A composite index on (a, b) can efficiently serve a query filtering only on
explanation: The index is ordered by a first, so a prefix of the column list is usable and a suffix is not. This leftmost-prefix rule decides column order when you design the index.

stem: A clustered index differs from a non-clustered one in that it

options.text: Determines the physical order of the rows, so there can be only one

explanation: Because the data is the index, range scans on the clustered key are very cheap and a poorly chosen clustered key is expensive to change later.

stem: A covering index speeds a query up by

options.text: Containing every column the query needs, so the table itself is never read

explanation: Avoiding the lookup back into the table can be a large win on wide tables. The cost is a wider index that is slower to maintain on writes.

stem: A standard SQL view is

options.text: A stored query that runs when the view is referenced

explanation: It provides abstraction and access control without duplicating data, and it costs whatever the underlying query costs each time. A materialised view is the variant that does store results.

stem: A materialised view differs from a standard view in that it

options.text: Stores the query result, trading staleness for read speed

explanation: The design question becomes refresh policy: how stale may the data be, and what does refreshing cost. That trade is the reason to choose one over the other.

stem: A database trigger executes

options.text: Automatically in response to an insert, update or delete

explanation: Because it fires implicitly, logic placed in a trigger is easy to miss when debugging. That invisibility is the main argument for keeping business rules in application code.

stem: A stored procedure differs from a trigger in that it

options.text: Is invoked explicitly by name rather than firing automatically

explanation: Explicit invocation makes the control flow visible to whoever reads the calling code, which is why procedures are easier to reason about than triggers.

stem: A savepoint inside a transaction allows

options.text: Rolling back to a marked point without abandoning the whole transaction

explanation: Nothing becomes durable until the outer commit, so a savepoint is a partial undo rather than a partial commit. It is useful for retrying one step of a long transaction.

stem: The CAP theorem states that during a network partition a distributed store must choose between
explanation: The choice only arises during a partition; the rest of the time a system can offer both. Treating CAP as a permanent pick-two is the most common misreading.

stem: Eventual consistency means

options.text: Replicas converge to the same value once updates stop, but may differ in the meantime

explanation: It is a liveness guarantee about convergence, not about how stale a read may be right now. Whether that is acceptable depends entirely on what the application does with the value.

stem: Sharding a database primarily addresses

options.text: Capacity, by splitting data across nodes on a shard key

explanation: The shard key decides everything downstream: queries that include it stay on one node, and queries that do not must fan out. Choosing it badly is expensive to undo.

stem: A FULL OUTER JOIN returns

options.text: Every row from both tables, with nulls where there is no match

explanation: It is the union of the left and right outer joins. It is the right tool for reconciliation, where you need to see records missing from either side.

stem: A CROSS JOIN produces

options.text: Every combination of rows from both tables

explanation: An omitted join condition produces the same result accidentally, which is the usual explanation for a query that suddenly returns millions of rows.

stem: A self join is used to

options.text: Join a table to itself, typically to relate rows within the same table

explanation: The classic case is an employee table with a manager_id referring to the same table. Aliasing each instance is what makes the query readable.

stem: The order in which you write joins in a standard SQL query

options.text: Is usually rearranged by the optimiser based on statistics

explanation: You express intent; the planner chooses the physical plan. This is why fixing a slow query usually means improving statistics or indexes rather than reordering the text.

stem: GROUP BY department, role produces one row per

options.text: Distinct combination of department and role

explanation: Grouping is on the tuple of listed columns. Expecting nested groups is a common misreading — SQL produces a flat result, and hierarchy is a presentation concern.

stem: HAVING used without GROUP BY

options.text: Treats the whole result as a single group

explanation: You can write HAVING COUNT(*) > 100 with no grouping to test the whole table. It is legal and occasionally useful, though usually a sign the query means something else.

stem: To find the department with the highest average salary you generally need

options.text: A subquery or window function, since you cannot nest aggregates directly

explanation: AVG of MAX is not permitted because the two collapse at different levels. Computing the averages first and then selecting the maximum over them is the shape that works.

stem: COUNT(DISTINCT col) differs from COUNT(col) in that it

options.text: Counts unique non-null values rather than all non-null values

explanation: Both ignore nulls; only the distinct form deduplicates, usually at the cost of a sort or hash. That cost is worth knowing before adding it to a large query.

stem: A correlated subquery differs from an ordinary one in that it

options.text: References a column from the outer query, so it is evaluated per outer row

explanation: The per-row evaluation is what makes it potentially expensive, though optimisers often rewrite it as a join. Recognising the correlation is the first step in diagnosing a slow query.

stem: EXISTS is often preferred over IN with a subquery because it

options.text: Can stop at the first match and is not broken by nulls in the subquery

explanation: IN must materialise or scan the list and NOT IN collapses on a null. EXISTS short-circuits and has no null pathology, which makes it the safer default for anti-joins.

stem: INTERSECT returns

options.text: Rows present in both result sets

explanation: EXCEPT, called MINUS in some engines, returns rows in the first and not the second. Set operators require the two queries to have matching column counts and compatible types.

stem: A column alias defined in SELECT can be referenced in
explanation: ORDER BY is logically evaluated after SELECT so the alias exists; WHERE runs before it and must repeat the expression. Knowing the logical order of clauses explains most such rules.

stem: In SQL LIKE, the wildcard matching exactly one character is
explanation: Percent matches any number of characters including none, and underscore matches exactly one. The shell-style wildcards are a common wrong answer.

stem: A CASE expression in SQL

options.text: Returns a value and may appear anywhere an expression is allowed

explanation: Being an expression is what lets it sit inside SELECT, ORDER BY and even aggregates, which is how conditional counting is written.

stem: COALESCE(a, b, 0) returns

options.text: Null if any argument is null

explanation: It is the standard way to supply a default for a nullable column. NULLIF is its counterpart, converting a specific value back to null.

stem: AVG over a column containing nulls computes the average over

options.text: All rows, treating null as zero

explanation: The denominator is the count of non-null values, so nulls raise the average relative to treating them as zero. Deciding which behaviour you want is a modelling decision, not a syntax one.

stem: Declaring a primary key usually also

options.text: Creates a unique index to enforce it

explanation: The constraint needs a fast uniqueness check, which the index provides. Adding a separate unique index on the same columns is therefore redundant.

stem: ON DELETE CASCADE means that deleting a parent row

options.text: Also deletes the referencing child rows

explanation: It is convenient and easy to underestimate: a single delete can remove a large subtree. ON DELETE SET NULL and RESTRICT are the alternatives worth considering first.

stem: A query filtering on UPPER(email) cannot use a plain index on email because

options.text: The index stores the raw column, not the function's result

explanation: Wrapping an indexed column in a function makes the predicate non-sargable. An expression index on UPPER(email), or storing a normalised column, restores the index.

stem: RANK and DENSE_RANK differ in that

options.text: RANK leaves gaps after a tie while DENSE_RANK does not

explanation: Two rows tied at rank 1 are followed by rank 3 under RANK and rank 2 under DENSE_RANK. ROW_NUMBER breaks ties arbitrarily and never repeats a value.

stem: PARTITION BY in a window function

options.text: Restarts the window calculation for each group, without collapsing rows

explanation: It is the windowing analogue of GROUP BY, except the input rows survive. This is how you produce a per-department running total alongside each employee row.

stem: A system call is expensive relative to a function call because it

options.text: Switches from user mode to kernel mode, with the associated state save and validation

explanation: The mode switch and argument validation cost far more than a jump. This is why buffered I/O exists: it amortises one system call over many logical operations.

stem: A zombie process is one that has

options.text: Terminated but whose exit status has not yet been collected by its parent

explanation: It holds only a process-table entry until the parent reaps it. An orphan is the different case where the parent exited first and init adopts the child.

stem: Which is NOT a standard inter-process communication mechanism?
explanation: Separate address spaces are exactly what makes direct argument passing impossible, which is why IPC mechanisms exist. Shared memory is the fastest of them and needs its own synchronisation.

stem: Shortest-job-first minimises average waiting time but is impractical because

options.text: It is unfair to short jobs
Job durations are not known in advance, and long jobs can starve

explanation: It is used as a theoretical optimum against which real schedulers are compared. Ageing, which raises a waiting job's priority over time, is the standard remedy for starvation.

stem: Priority inversion occurs when

options.text: A high-priority task waits on a lock held by a low-priority task that is itself preempted

explanation: Priority inheritance temporarily raises the lock holder's priority so it can finish and release. The Mars Pathfinder fault is the famous case study.

stem: A preemptive scheduler differs from a cooperative one in that it

options.text: Can interrupt a running task without its cooperation

explanation: Cooperative scheduling depends on every task yielding, so one misbehaving task freezes the system. Preemption needs a timer interrupt, which is what makes it robust.

stem: A spinlock is preferable to a blocking mutex when

options.text: The expected wait is shorter than the cost of a context switch

explanation: Spinning burns CPU, so it only pays when the wait is very short and a core is available. Using one around a long or blocking section is a serious performance bug.

stem: The producer-consumer problem requires

options.text: A bounded buffer with synchronisation for both full and empty conditions

explanation: Two condition variables, or two counting semaphores plus a mutex, handle the two distinct waits. Using a single condition for both is a classic source of missed wakeups.

stem: Starvation differs from deadlock in that a starving process

options.text: Could still run, but is repeatedly passed over

explanation: Deadlock is a permanent circular wait; starvation is a scheduling unfairness that could resolve. Ageing fixes starvation and does nothing for deadlock.

stem: The banker's algorithm avoids deadlock by

options.text: Granting a request only if the resulting state is still safe

explanation: It requires each process to declare its maximum need up front, which is why it is rarely practical outside teaching. Detection and recovery is what real systems use.

stem: Internal fragmentation is wasted space

options.text: Inside an allocated block, because the allocation was rounded up

explanation: Paging removes external fragmentation and introduces internal fragmentation in the final partial page. Segmentation has the opposite profile, which is why many systems combine the two.

stem: The translation lookaside buffer caches
explanation: Without it every memory access would need an extra walk of the page table. A TLB miss is one of the hidden costs of a context switch, since the entries are often invalidated.

stem: Demand paging loads a page

options.text: When it is first accessed, triggering a page fault

explanation: This makes startup fast and memory use proportional to what is actually touched. The first access to each page pays a fault, which is why warm-up matters for latency-sensitive services.

stem: Real systems approximate LRU rather than implementing it exactly because

options.text: Exact LRU requires updating an ordering on every memory access, which is too expensive

explanation: The clock or second-chance algorithm uses a single reference bit per page and a rotating pointer, which is close enough at a tiny fraction of the cost.

stem: An inode stores

options.text: The file's metadata and the location of its data blocks

explanation: Names live in directory entries that point at inodes, which is why one file can have several hard links. Deleting a name only frees the file when the last link and open handle are gone.

stem: A journaling file system improves crash recovery by

options.text: Writing intended changes to a log before applying them, so recovery can replay or discard

explanation: Recovery becomes a short log scan rather than a full consistency check of the whole volume. Most implementations journal metadata only by default, which is a durability trade.

stem: A hard link differs from a symbolic link in that it

options.text: Points to the inode directly, so the file survives deleting the original name

explanation: A symbolic link stores a path and dangles if the target moves; a hard link is another name for the same inode. Hard links cannot cross file systems because inode numbers are per-volume.

stem: A thread pool is used instead of creating a thread per task because

options.text: Threads cannot be created at run time
Thread creation is expensive and unbounded concurrency exhausts resources

explanation: The pool amortises creation and, more importantly, bounds concurrency so a spike in work does not exhaust memory or thrash the scheduler.

stem: HTTP, DNS and SMTP all operate at which OSI layer?
explanation: They define message formats and semantics for programs, and rely on the transport layer beneath for delivery. Mapping named protocols to layers is a standard one-mark question.

stem: TCP flow control and congestion control differ in that flow control protects

options.text: The receiver from being overwhelmed, while congestion control protects the network

explanation: Flow control is driven by the receiver's advertised window; congestion control is inferred by the sender from loss and delay. The two operate simultaneously and limit the sending rate independently.

stem: TCP connection teardown normally takes

options.text: Four steps, because each direction is closed independently

explanation: FIN and ACK in each direction allow a half-closed state where one side has finished sending but still receives. The TIME_WAIT state afterwards exists to absorb delayed duplicates.

stem: Nagle's algorithm improves efficiency by

options.text: Coalescing small writes into fewer segments

explanation: It reduces header overhead on chatty connections and adds latency to small interactive messages, which is why latency-sensitive applications disable it.

stem: A host with address 192.168.10.130 and mask 255.255.255.192 belongs to which network?
explanation: A /26 mask makes blocks of 64, so the boundaries are .0, .64, .128 and .192. The address falls in the block starting at .128, whose broadcast is .191.

stem: In CIDR notation, a larger prefix length means

options.text: Fewer host addresses, because more bits identify the network

explanation: Each additional prefix bit halves the host space, so a /24 holds 254 usable hosts and a /25 holds 126. The relationship being inverse is what catches people out.

stem: Network address translation allows

options.text: Many private addresses to share one public address

explanation: It was widely adopted to conserve scarce IPv4 addresses, and it breaks unsolicited inbound connections, which is why port forwarding exists.

stem: A recursive DNS resolver differs from an authoritative server in that it

options.text: Queries other servers on the client's behalf until it has an answer

explanation: Authoritative servers hold the records for their zone; resolvers walk the hierarchy and cache what they learn. TTL values on records control how long that cache is valid.

stem: Which record maps a hostname to another hostname rather than to an address?
explanation: A and AAAA map to IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, MX names a mail server, and TXT holds arbitrary text used for verification. CNAME is an alias, and it cannot coexist with other records at the same name.

stem: UDP has lower overhead than TCP partly because its header lacks
explanation: No sequencing means no reordering, no retransmission and no connection state to keep. The eight-byte header against TCP's twenty is the visible consequence.

stem: During a TLS handshake, the server's certificate is used to

options.text: Authenticate the server and establish a shared symmetric key

explanation: Asymmetric cryptography authenticates and agrees the key; the bulk data is then encrypted symmetrically because it is far faster. Assuming the certificate encrypts the traffic is a common misconception.

stem: An HTTP GET is expected to be

options.text: Idempotent and safe, causing no server-side change

explanation: Safety means no intended side effect, which is why intermediaries may cache and retry GETs freely. A GET that mutates state breaks assumptions all the way through the stack.

stem: An HTTP 502 indicates

options.text: An upstream server returned an invalid response to a gateway
The client sent a bad request

explanation: The 5xx class is server-side. 502 and 504 both point at the upstream rather than at the gateway itself, which is useful when deciding where to look first.

stem: A switch differs from a router in that it forwards based on

options.text: MAC addresses, within a single network segment

explanation: Switching is layer two and local; routing is layer three and between networks. A device sold as a home router usually performs both functions plus NAT.

stem: A router separates broadcast domains, whereas a switch by default

options.text: Forwards broadcasts to every port in the segment

explanation: This is why large flat networks suffer from broadcast traffic, and why VLANs exist to subdivide a switch into separate domains.

stem: ping uses which protocol?
explanation: ICMP carries control and diagnostic messages and has no ports, which is why a firewall rule for it looks different from one for TCP or UDP. A blocked ping does not mean the host is down.

stem: HTTPS conventionally uses port
explanation: 80 is HTTP, 22 is SSH and 25 is SMTP. These are conventions registered with IANA, not enforced by the protocols, so a service can run on any port.

stem: A stateful firewall differs from a stateless packet filter in that it

options.text: Tracks connections, so return traffic for an allowed outbound flow is permitted automatically

explanation: Connection tracking is what makes rule sets manageable: you allow the outbound connection and the replies follow. A stateless filter needs explicit rules for both directions.

stem: git fetch differs from git pull in that fetch

options.text: Downloads remote changes without merging them into your branch

explanation: Fetching then inspecting before merging is the safer habit, because pull does both in one step and can produce a merge you did not expect.

stem: git cherry-pick is used to

options.text: Apply a specific commit from one branch onto another

explanation: It creates a new commit with a different hash, so the change exists twice in history. Overusing it on long-lived branches leads to confusing duplicate changes.

stem: A detached HEAD state means

options.text: HEAD points at a commit rather than a branch, so new commits belong to no branch

explanation: Commits made there are reachable only by hash and can be garbage collected. Creating a branch before leaving is how you keep them.

stem: The rule 'never rebase a public branch' exists because rebasing

options.text: Rewrites commit hashes, so anyone who pulled the old history diverges

explanation: Everyone based on the old commits has to reconcile a history that no longer exists. Rebasing your own unpushed work is exactly the case the rule leaves open.

stem: Squashing commits before merging aims to

options.text: Present the change as one coherent commit in the mainline history

explanation: It trades the detailed development history for a readable mainline. Teams differ on whether that trade is worth it, which is why it is a convention rather than a rule.

stem: Adding a file to .gitignore after it has already been committed

options.text: Has no effect until it is removed from tracking

explanation: Ignore rules apply to untracked files only. Removing it from the index with git rm --cached is the missing step, and the file remains in past commits either way.

stem: git bisect finds the commit that introduced a bug by

options.text: Binary searching the history, asking you to test each midpoint

explanation: It reduces hundreds of commits to a handful of tests. Automating the test with git bisect run turns it into a single command.

stem: Test-driven development prescribes writing

options.text: A failing test first, then the minimum code to pass it, then refactoring

explanation: The failing test first is what guarantees the test can actually fail, which an after-the-fact test does not establish. The refactor step is the one most often dropped.

stem: A mock differs from a stub in that a mock

options.text: Verifies that the expected interactions occurred

explanation: A stub supplies canned answers so the test can proceed; a mock additionally asserts on how it was called. Over-mocking couples tests to implementation detail and makes refactoring painful.

stem: A test that passes and fails without code changes should be

options.text: Treated as a defect and fixed, because it destroys trust in the whole suite

explanation: A suite people ignore protects nothing, and tolerating one flaky test normalises re-running until green. The usual causes are time, ordering and shared state.

stem: The primary value of code review is

options.text: Catching design and correctness problems a compiler cannot, and spreading knowledge

explanation: Formatting belongs to an automated formatter, which frees the review for questions only a human can answer. The knowledge-sharing effect is often the larger long-term benefit.

stem: Under semantic versioning, a breaking API change requires incrementing the
explanation: Minor is for backwards-compatible additions and patch for backwards-compatible fixes. The contract is what lets dependents choose an update policy safely.

stem: A feature flag decouples

options.text: Deploying code from releasing the behaviour to users

explanation: Merged-but-dark code can ship continuously and be enabled gradually. The cost is flag debt: every flag is a branch in the code that must eventually be removed.

stem: A blue-green deployment reduces risk by

options.text: Running two environments and switching traffic, so rollback is a switch back

explanation: Rollback becomes near-instant because the previous version is still running. The cost is double the infrastructure and care with shared state such as the database.

stem: Technical debt is best understood as

options.text: Bad code written by careless people
A deliberate or accidental shortcut whose ongoing interest is paid in slower future change

explanation: The metaphor's point is the interest: the shortcut keeps costing until it is repaid. Framing it that way makes the case for repayment in terms a stakeholder can weigh.
